newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices steady after short-lived rally.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices steady after short-lived rally.

text.p: World oil prices were steady on Wednesday after U.S. energy stocks data spurred an earlier rally, which evaporated later on continued signs of healthy physical supply, traders said.

"There are some people hoping that crude has found a floor and technically maybe it has but fundamentally, given physical demand, the market is seen as oversupplied," said Charles Gray of Prudential Bache securities in London.
World marker crude Brent Blend for April delivery traded just two cents up on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) at 1632 GMT, having achieved a morning session high of $19.73 a barrel.
The latest rally began on Tuesday, ahead of publication by the American Petroleum Institute (API) of its weekly U.S. inventory figures. April Brent settled 58 cents higher on Tuesday.

The API figures released after markets closed on Tuesday showed surprise falls in both crude oil and gasoline stocks, the latter crucial at this time of year in the run-up to the U.S. summer driving season.
Information released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) on Wednesday confirmed the bullish picture.
But traders said the news was already factored into prices and was good only for a brief rally.
"What we typically see after the U.S. data are released is that the market rallies for the first 15-45 minutes. But the shelf life of the APIs seems to be half an hour," Gray said.
Brent fell to an eight-month low of $18.68 on Monday as the market continued a headlong slide in prices which has seen Brent plummet by nearly $6 from the year's high of $24.91 hit in January.

A mild end to the northern hemisphere winter, which has stunted demand for heating oil and allowed global inventories to recover from historically low levels, and rising output from producers both inside and outside the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), lay behind the steep price slide.
A survey by Reuters on Wednesday showed that production from countries outside OPEC accelerated in 1996, rising 840,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 39.28 million bpd.

This was in fact lower than most analysts expected for non-OPEC growth for last year. Delays to new field start-ups, Iraq's continued absence from oil markets up until December last year and low stocks all helped to propel prices to a near six-year high last October.
